source: Shannon (1948) A Mathematical Theory of Communication
finding: Shannon asks for a measure H(p1..pn) of how much choice or uncertainty there is among events with known probabilities. He lists three demands: H is continuous; with equal probabilities H grows with n; and H is the weighted sum when a choice is split into two steps. Theorem 2 says the only H meeting these is H = -K sum p_i log p_i.
numbers: Worked split example: H(1/2,1/3,1/6) = H(1/2,1/2) + 1/2 H(2/3,1/3). Three axioms only. K sets the unit (bits for log base 2).
quote: The only H satisfying the three above assumptions is of the form
limits: Shannon says the theorem is not necessary for the theory; the real justification is its implications. The axioms make entropy plausible, they do not prove it is the only sensible uncertainty measure.
agent_relevance: Formal basis for scoring a probe by the uncertainty it removes (S7). The additivity axiom lets a multi-step question plan be scored as a sum of step gains.

source: Shannon (1948) A Mathematical Theory of Communication
finding: The source is modelled as a Markov process. Entropy per symbol is defined through F_N, the conditional entropy of the next symbol given N-1 previous ones, and G_N, the block entropy per symbol. Both converge to H. If no influence reaches beyond N symbols, F_N = H.
numbers: Relative entropy = H / Hmax = the maximum compression possible in the same alphabet. Redundancy = 1 - relative entropy.
limits: Stationary ergodic source assumed. Real text and real problem streams are not stationary.
agent_relevance: Entropy is defined relative to a model of the source. Every entropy estimate the agent makes depends on the model that supplies the probabilities (see a10, a11).

source: Shannon (1948) A Mathematical Theory of Communication
finding: A ladder of approximations to English over a 27-symbol alphabet shows how added context lowers apparent randomness: zero order (XFOML RXKHRJFFJUJ ...), first order, digram, trigram, then first- and second-order word approximations. Resemblance to English rises at each step, and samples look sensible to about twice the construction range.
numbers: Six levels, 27 symbols (26 letters and space). Word-level sample: THE HEAD AND IN FRONTAL ATTACK ON AN ENGLISH WRITER THAT THE CHARACTER OF THIS POINT ...
limits: Qualitative demonstration, not a measurement. Local statistics give local fluency only.
agent_relevance: The same ladder is the old picture of a language model: more context, lower entropy, better text. Local fluency is not global validity, so low per-token surprise is not proof of a right answer.

source: Shannon (1948) A Mathematical Theory of Communication
finding: Redundancy of English is roughly 50 percent when structure over about 8 letters is counted. Shannon says three independent methods agree: entropy of the approximations, restoring deleted letters, and cryptography. Basic English (850 words) has very high redundancy; Finnegans Wake has little.
numbers: Redundancy about 50 percent; if text with 50 percent of letters deleted can be restored, redundancy exceeds 50 percent.
limits: Limited to about 8 letter range. Shannon's own 1951 paper revises this upward (a08).
agent_relevance: Redundancy is the room a prover or probe can exploit. A very redundant problem statement needs few probes; a low-redundancy one needs many.

source: Shannon (1948) A Mathematical Theory of Communication
finding: Noiseless coding theorem (Theorem 9): a source with entropy H bits per symbol can be encoded for a channel of capacity C bits per second to send at average rate C/H - epsilon symbols per second, and not faster than C/H. Theorem 3 splits long sequences into a high-probability typical set and a small-probability remainder.
numbers: Rate limit = C/H symbols per second. Epsilon arbitrarily small.
limits: Asymptotic. Needs long blocks and known source statistics. Does not say how to build the code.
agent_relevance: Code length of an outcome is about -log2 p. This is the link from probability to description length that MDL uses (subfield 03).

source: Shannon (1948) A Mathematical Theory of Communication
finding: Noisy channel: equivocation H_y(x) is the uncertainty about what was sent that remains after seeing what was received. Capacity C = max (H(x) - H_y(x)). Theorem 11: if the source rate H is at most C, errors can be made arbitrarily small by coding; if H exceeds C, equivocation cannot go below H - C.
numbers: Rate of transmission R = H(x) - H_y(x). Theorem 17: for white thermal noise of power N and signal power P, band W, C = W log((P+N)/N).
limits: Existence proof, not a construction. Assumes a known noise model.
agent_relevance: A probe or test is a noisy channel from truth to observation. Information gained = prior entropy minus remaining equivocation. That is expected information gain as a probe score (a19, a21).

source: Shannon (1951) Prediction and Entropy of Printed English
finding: Shannon estimated the entropy of English from n-gram tables and from word frequencies before turning to human prediction. Letter entropies: F0 = 4.7, F1 = 4.14, F2 = 3.56 bits per letter. A Zipf word-frequency estimate gives 11.82 bits per word, which is 2.62 bits per letter at 4.5 letters per word. The 1948 figure was about 2.3 bits at 8-letter range.
limits: 26-letter alphabet, spaces and punctuation ignored for these figures. Uses 1942 letter-count tables.
agent_relevance: Shows a model-based way to estimate uncertainty: more context in the model, lower estimated entropy. The estimate always depends on the context the model sees.

source: Shannon (1951) Prediction and Entropy of Printed English
finding: Shannon had people predict text: the subject guesses the next letter until right, and the number of guesses gives bounds on entropy. As the subject sees more preceding text, both bounds fall. The conclusion is entropy of the order of one bit per letter with 100 letters of context, redundancy about 75 percent.
numbers: Upper bound by letters of context (N=1,2,3,4,100): 4.03, 3.42, 3.0, 2.6, about 1.3. Lower bound: 3.19, 2.50, 2.1, 1.7, about 0.6. Example passage: 79 of 102 symbols right on first guess.
limits: Very small sample; helpers were Mrs Shannon and Dr Oliver. The lower bound was proved only for an ideal predictor; Shannon admits sampling error. The table text extracted by OCR is imperfect, so the N=100 digits should be checked against the page.
agent_relevance: Humans reach about 1 bit per character with long context. Models are measured against this (Brown 1992, a10; modern LLM compression, a11).

source: Shannon (1951) Prediction and Entropy of Printed English
finding: Shannon proves the bounds from guess-rank frequencies. The upper bound follows because the entropy is largest when predictions are spread as in the observed rank frequencies, and holds whether or not the prediction is ideal. The lower bound needs a rectangular decomposition argument and is proved only for an ideal predictor.
numbers: Upper bound valid for any predictor; lower bound for ideal prediction only.
limits: Human subjects are not ideal predictors. Shannon argues the error from non-rectangular conditional distributions more than offsets the error from non-ideal humans.
agent_relevance: A bound built from a model's own guess distribution is only as sound as that model's calibration. This applies to LLM self-reported probabilities.

source: Brown, Della Pietra, deSouza, Lai, Mercer (1992) An Estimate of an Upper Bound for the Entropy of English
finding: A word trigram model trained on about 583 million words gives an upper bound of 1.75 bits per character on the 5.96 million character Brown Corpus. It is a cross-entropy, so a true upper bound, and rests on a far larger sample than Shannon's human test.
numbers: 1.75 bits per character. Training text 582.755 million words. Test: Brown Corpus, 5.96 million characters, 95 printable ASCII characters. Baselines: 8 bits ASCII, 7 bits packed, 4.46 Huffman, 4.43 Unix compress, 4.20 Miller-Wegman adaptive Lempel-Ziv.
quote: Our bound is higher than previous entropy estimates, but it is statistically more reliable
limits: Higher than the Shannon-era human estimates, and the authors say people probably predict better than their simple trigram model. Different corpus and alphabet (95 characters with case and spacing) from Shannon's 27 symbols.
agent_relevance: Cross-entropy of a model on held-out text needs no humans. A better model gives a tighter bound. This is the basis of using log-loss as an uncertainty measure.

source: Delétang et al. (2024) Language Modeling Is Compression (ICLR 2024)
finding: Large language models used with arithmetic coding are general lossless compressors, even for images and audio they were not trained on. Chinchilla 70B compresses ImageNet patches to 43.4 percent and LibriSpeech samples to 16.4 percent of raw size, beating PNG (58.5) and FLAC (30.3). On text (enwik9) Chinchilla 70B reaches 8.3 percent and Llama 2 7B 8.9 percent, against gzip 32.3 and LZMA2 23.0.
numbers: Raw compression rate on enwik9, chunk 2048 bytes: gzip 32.3, LZMA2 23.0, Transformer 3.2M 17.0, Llama 2 7B 8.9, Chinchilla 1B 11.3, 7B 10.2, 70B 8.3. Random data stays near 100 percent for classical compressors.
limits: The raw rate ignores model size. With parameters counted (adjusted rate), Chinchilla 70B on enwik9 is 21.9 percent and on ImageNet, LibriSpeech and random data the adjusted rates are above 100 percent. Small Transformers trained on enwik8 overfit to that modality.
agent_relevance: Log-loss equals code length. A model's per-token surprise is the description length of the data under that model, so uncertainty and compression are one quantity.

source: Delétang et al. (2024) Language Modeling Is Compression, scaling and tokenization
finding: Larger models compress larger datasets better, but do worse on small datasets once their own size is counted: dataset size sets a hard limit on useful model size. Tokenization acts as a pre-compression and in general does not improve the final compression rate.
numbers: Model size counted as 2 bytes per parameter (float16). Adjusted rate = log-loss plus model size (two-part code). Vanilla Transformers of several sizes trained on enwik8.
limits: Offline setting. Small Transformers on one dataset; each dataset has a critical model size after which the adjusted rate rises again.
agent_relevance: Two-part code (model plus data) is the MDL objective. A bigger rule or scaffold pays only if the data it explains is large enough (G7).

source: Delétang et al. (2024) Language Modeling Is Compression, framing
finding: The paper recalls that a good predictor gives a good compressor and the reverse. Optimal prediction by the Solomonoff predictor corresponds to optimal compression, and a model that compresses well generalises well.
numbers: Solomonoff predictor and the Hutter prize for compressing human knowledge are cited; no new figures.
limits: Framing section. Solomonoff induction is incomputable.
agent_relevance: Ties Shannon entropy to Kolmogorov complexity and MDL (subfields 02, 03).

source: Hoffmann et al. (2022) Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models (Chinchilla)
finding: Final loss is fitted as L(N,D) = E + A/N^alpha + B/D^beta. The authors say the constant term E should correspond to the entropy of natural text, the loss of an ideal generative process.
limits: E is a fitted constant for their tokenizer and data mix. It is not a measured entropy of English and cannot be compared with Shannon's bits per letter without conversion.
agent_relevance: Even a perfect model keeps an irreducible uncertainty floor. A probe aimed at noise, not at reducible ignorance, gains nothing (see a22).

source: Kuhn, Gal, Farquhar (2023) Semantic Uncertainty: Linguistic Invariances for Uncertainty Estimation in NLG (ICLR 2023)
finding: Token-level entropy treats two wordings of one meaning as different outcomes. Semantic entropy clusters sampled answers by bidirectional entailment, then takes the entropy over meanings. It predicts whether an answer is correct better than predictive entropy, length-normalised entropy, lexical similarity and p(True).
numbers: OPT 2.7B to 30B on TriviaQA and CoQA (8000 questions each). The entailment equivalence check was 92.7 percent accurate on TriviaQA and 95.5 percent on CoQA (300 hand-labelled generations). Table 2, rows as printed: distinct meanings 1.27 correct vs 1.77 incorrect, AUROC 0.77 for semantic entropy vs 0.66 for the count; 1.89 vs 3.89, AUROC 0.83 vs 0.79.
quote: Adjusting for semantic equivalence in this way offers better uncertainty estimation than standard entropy
limits: OPT-era models only. Needs M samples and pairwise entailment calls, so cost grows with M. Row-to-dataset order in Table 2 not confirmed from the extracted text.
agent_relevance: Count meaning clusters, not strings. A probe whose answer is uncertain only between paraphrases is not uncertain.

source: Kuhn, Gal, Farquhar (2023) Semantic Uncertainty, sampling trade-off
finding: Entropy estimates from sampled answers need samples that are both accurate and diverse. Lower temperature raises answer accuracy, higher temperature raises diversity, and the best AUROC for semantic entropy and length-normalised entropy is at temperature 0.5.
numbers: Best temperature 0.5 (TriviaQA, OPT 30B, Fig. 3b).
limits: One model family. The authors say this tuning strengthens the baselines compared with earlier implementations.
agent_relevance: Sampling settings are a tuning choice. Test temperature before trusting any entropy estimate of agent confidence.

source: Farquhar, Kossen, Kuhn, Gal (2024) Detecting hallucinations in large language models using semantic entropy, Nature 630
finding: Semantic entropy detects confabulations, answers that are arbitrary and change between runs. Averaged over 30 task and model combinations it reaches AUROC 0.790, against naive entropy 0.691, P(True) 0.698 and an embedding regression baseline 0.687. It also works on GPT-4 paragraph-length biographies and on maths word problems.
numbers: AUROC 0.790 vs 0.691 / 0.698 / 0.687; stable between 0.78 and 0.81 across settings; average over five runs.
quote: does not help when LLM outputs are systematically bad
limits: The authors say it catches confabulations only, and does not help when a model is consistently wrong because of bad training data or systematic failure. Needs several samples per question.
agent_relevance: Disagreement between samples is a signal that code can read (a trigger for G1). Low semantic entropy is a hint, not proof (G4).

source: Kossen et al. (2024) Semantic Entropy Probes: Robust and Cheap Hallucination Detection in LLMs
finding: Linear probes on hidden states predict semantic entropy from a single generation, cutting the 5 to 10 fold sampling cost. They work even before any answer token is generated, and generalise to unseen tasks better than probes trained to predict accuracy.
numbers: AUROC for predicting binarised semantic entropy from hidden states: 0.7 to 0.95 depending on model, layer and task. SEP minus accuracy probe in-distribution (AUROC x100): Mistral-7B +2.8, Phi-3-3.8B +2.1, Llama-2-7B -0.5, Llama-2-70B +1.3 (short form); Llama-2-70B -1.9, Llama-3-70B -2.0 (long form).
limits: Open models of 3B to 70B only. Accuracy probes win in-distribution on most layers and tasks except NQ Open. Very high BioASQ AUROC may reflect probes detecting the yes/no question type.
agent_relevance: With hidden-state access, uncertainty before answering is cheap. With an API-only model it is not, and sampling is the fallback.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts: Uncertainty-Aware Planning Enhances Information Seeking in LLMs
finding: UoT simulates future question and answer branches, scores each question by expected information gain over the set of possible hypotheses, and propagates reward through the tree. Across 20 Questions, medical diagnosis and troubleshooting it raises success rate by 38.1 percent on average over direct prompting, across 5 LLMs.
numbers: Mean +38.1 percent over direct prompting (DP); Llama3-70B +46.6 percent. Beats CoT-SC by 33.8 percent and Reflexion by 29.9; beats original ToT by 28.3 and adapted ToT by 12.4. GPT-4, DX 97.0 percent, MedDG 88.0, FloDial 67.3 (up from 43.7). Llama3-70B closed-set 20Q Common 55.9 vs DP 51.4; Thing 25.0 vs 15.0.
limits: Reward is a modified IG with a sharpening hyperparameter, because raw IG did not separate branches enough. Assumes answers exclude hypotheses cleanly; the authors note that 'no fever' does not fully rule out COVID. Benchmarks are simplified, mainly closed hypothesis sets.
agent_relevance: Entropy reduction as the rule for choosing a probe, tested on LLMs, with gains over generic reasoning methods. The closest published match to the S7 probe-choice idea.

source: Bertolazzi, Mazzaccara, Merlo, Bernardi (2023) ChatGPT's Information Seeking Strategy: Insights from the 20-Questions Game
finding: On small hypothesis sets ChatGPT is close to an optimal half-split on turn 1, but later questions lose informativeness. It keeps asking after the target is already identified, and asks trivial questions. Telling it to update the candidate list stepwise improves play.
numbers: 8-candidate games: ChatGPT averages 7.24 questions per game; 73.77 percent constraint-seeking and 26.33 percent hypothesis-scanning questions. The optimal agent uses log2(N) - 1 constraint-seeking questions then 1 or 2 hypothesis-scanning ones (57.14 / 42.86 percent). In 56.67 percent of games questions continued after one candidate remained; 29.29 percent of questions were unnecessary; 39.44 percent of second questions were trivial. Annotation accuracy 83 percent on 180 questions.
limits: Hierarchical candidate sets of 8 and 16, ChatGPT of early 2023. Wilcoxon tests, p < 0.001 against the optimal agent. Newer models are stronger (see a21).
agent_relevance: The model asks a good first probe and then fails to track the remaining hypothesis set. The program, not the model, should hold the candidate set and compute the split.

source: Choudhury, Williamson et al. (2026) BED-LLM (ICLR 2026)
finding: Choosing each question by estimated expected information gain, with the LLM supplying the probability model, beats asking the LLM for a good question. On 20 Questions it lifts success by 37.4 percentage points on average over direct prompting; success more than doubles in over half the setups and never drops.
numbers: Animals, success after 20 turns: GPT-4o-mini Prompt-Only 44, Split 78, CoT 55, BED-LLM 88; GPT-4o Prompt-Only 45, BED-LLM 93; Llama-3.1-8B Prompt-Only 8, BED-LLM 63. Binomial standard error about 3 to 5 points per cell.
limits: Table extracted by OCR. The hypothesis set is generated by the LLM and EIG is estimated by sampling, so it depends on how the joint model is updated and on LLM conditionals being faithful.
agent_relevance: Strongest recent result for entropy-guided probing with code doing the scoring. Supports G5 and S7.

source: Choudhury et al. (2026) BED-LLM, predictive entropy vs EIG
finding: Maximising raw predictive entropy of the answer is not the same as maximising information gain. A question can have a wholly uncertain answer and still teach nothing about the target (the ice-cream question in a film-preference task). Replacing full EIG by the marginal entropy term degrades results, and keeping the conditional-entropy term costs no extra LLM calls.
numbers: Animals, success: GPT-4o-mini BED-LLM 88 vs Entropy ablation 79 vs Split 78; GPT-4o 93 vs 88; Llama-3.1-8B 63 vs 54.
limits: One task family (20 Questions plus preference elicitation). The gap is 5 to 9 points in these rows.
agent_relevance: Do not pick the probe whose answer is most uncertain. Pick the one most informative about the hypothesis, subtracting the expected noise entropy.

source: Choudhury et al. (2026) BED-LLM, related work
finding: The authors state that modern LLMs write coherent single questions but struggle to tailor them to earlier answers in multi-turn tasks, citing Bertolazzi 2023 and others. Prior methods use restricted hypothesis spaces; BED-LLM lets the LLM generate them.
numbers: Introduction claim; no new numbers.
limits: Related-work summary, not an experiment.
agent_relevance: Agrees with a20: keep the hypothesis set in the program.

source: Li, Tamkin, Goodman, Andreas (2023) Eliciting Human Preferences with Language Models (GATE)
finding: LM-led elicitation (open questions, yes/no questions, generated edge cases) often draws out more usable information than user-written prompts or labelled examples, with less user effort. The human study used 388 Prolific participants across email validation, content recommendation and moral reasoning.
numbers: N = 388. Metric: area under the p(correct) vs time curve over 5 minutes. Average entropy in p(yes) across participants was 0.77 bits, so preferences really varied.
limits: Statistical significance over baselines only in content recommendation and email validation, not moral reasoning. Preregistered.
agent_relevance: Elicitation works only if uncertainty exists to remove. The 0.77 bits figure is a check that a probe has something to learn.

source: Li et al. (2023) GATE, pool-based active learning comparison
finding: Three pool-based active learning rules (random, diversity, uncertainty sampling) performed comparably, diversity possibly slightly better. The authors say this agrees with Margatina et al. 2023. So uncertainty sampling over a fixed pool did not clearly beat random here.
numbers: Three strategies compared in the appendix; no strong difference; diversity sampling used in the main human experiments.
limits: Fixed example pool, not free-form questions. Significance not reported in the text read.
agent_relevance: A caution: the most uncertain item is not guaranteed best. Diversity of probes may matter as much as raw entropy.

source: Cover and King (1978) A convergent gambling estimate of the entropy of English
finding: Cover and King replaced guess counting with a gambling method: subjects bet on the next letter and wealth growth gives an entropy estimate. Reported from memory as an upper bound near 1.3 bits per letter. Brown et al. cite it for the earlier bibliography.
numbers: About 1.3 bits per letter (memory only; paper not opened).
limits: Not opened this session. Number from memory; check before use. Small sample of human subjects.
agent_relevance: A betting-based elicitation turns subjective probability into a score, a precedent for proper scoring of agent self-estimates.

source: Lindley (1956) On a measure of the information provided by an experiment
finding: Lindley defined the expected information from an experiment as the expected drop in Shannon entropy of the parameter posterior. This is the root of expected information gain (EIG) in Bayesian experimental design.
numbers: No numbers (not opened).
limits: Not opened this session. Cited by Bertolazzi et al. for EIG. Requires a prior and a likelihood for each experiment.
agent_relevance: Formal definition behind the S7 probe rule: choose the probe with the largest expected posterior entropy reduction.

source: Oaksford and Chater (1994) A rational analysis of the selection task as optimal data selection
finding: Oaksford and Chater proposed that people choose cards in the Wason selection task to maximise expected information gain in Shannon terms, under a rarity assumption. This recasts the apparent logic error as sensible information seeking.
numbers: No numbers (not opened; summary from memory).
limits: Not opened this session. The account has been criticised and re-tested with mixed results; check before citing detail.
agent_relevance: Human probe choice may already follow entropy rules, a precedent for EIG as the default probe score.

source: Cover and Thomas (2006) Elements of Information Theory, 2nd ed.
finding: Standard textbook for entropy, mutual information, KL divergence and source coding. Mutual information I(X;Y) = H(X) - H(X|Y) is the quantity equal to expected information gain.
numbers: No numbers (not opened).
limits: Not opened this session.
agent_relevance: Reference for the identity: EIG equals mutual information between hypothesis and probe outcome.
